content:
Dear Quillstone AI Hiring Team,

I am applying for the Machine Learning Engineer – Customer Support AI role. As a Data Scientist moving into Machine Learning Engineering, I have built and operated scheduled forecasting and batch-scoring workflows in Python and SQL, and I am keen to bring that experience to AI systems that help merchants get support quickly and without friction.

At Thistlebox, I developed a six-week-ahead recipe-demand forecasting workflow using LightGBM, orchestrated as scheduled notebook jobs in Vertex AI Workbench, with outputs written to BigQuery for operational reporting. The workflow improved WAPE from 23% to 14%, with an estimated 9% reduction in food waste. I also built a weekly XGBoost churn-scoring workflow in BigQuery and validated retention targeting with a holdout, where churn decreased by 2.1 percentage points in the treated group. These projects have given me practical experience in feature engineering, evaluation and running repeatable ML workflows on GCP.

I have also added pytest unit tests for forecasting feature code, reaching approximately 60% coverage, and built and containerised a Python Streamlit application, writing its Dockerfile; the data platform team handled deployment to Cloud Run. My MSc in Statistics, including a dissertation on Bayesian hierarchical models, supports my modelling and experimental-design work. I am now looking to develop further as an ML engineer, contributing careful testing, ownership and practical problem-solving as I deepen my production engineering experience.

Quillstone’s focus on support automation and its emphasis on team ownership, open sharing and learning from feedback make this role especially appealing to me. I would welcome the opportunity to discuss how my experience with forecasting, churn modelling and data workflows could contribute to the AI team.

Kind regards,
Tobias Mwangi-Hartley

critique.content_quality_feedback: This is a clear, professional, and appropriately concise cover letter. It uses strong quantified evidence: WAPE improvement from 23% to 14%, estimated 9% food-waste reduction, a 2.1-percentage-point churn reduction, approximately 60% test coverage, and a user base of approximately 25 people. It also accurately explains the candidate's transition from Data Science into Machine Learning Engineering and does not overclaim API deployment or cloud-infrastructure ownership. The main content limitation is that the letter presents highly relevant transferable experience but cannot demonstrate several core Customer Support AI requirements.
critique.ats_compatibility_feedback: The letter is highly parseable: it uses conventional paragraphs, standard punctuation, no tables or graphics, and clearly names Python, SQL, GCP, BigQuery, Vertex AI Workbench, LightGBM, XGBoost, feature engineering, pytest, Docker, Streamlit, and Cloud Run. It also includes useful terms such as scheduled workflows, batch scoring, evaluation, and testing. For this particular vacancy, AI screening probability is moderate-to-low because the document does not contain supported evidence for chat assistants, RAG, language models, model serving, monitoring, data versioning, or the named MLOps platforms. These are candidate-experience gaps rather than keywords that should be added without evidence.
critique.job_alignment_feedback: The strongest alignment is with Python/SQL-based machine learning workflows, GCP, feature engineering, orchestration through scheduled jobs, batch scoring, model evaluation, automated testing, and practical ownership. The examples demonstrate measurable business impact and a credible transition toward ML engineering. The letter also aligns reasonably well with Quillstone's emphasis on ownership, practical problem-solving, learning, and feedback. However, the candidate's material shows gaps against several central requirements: the candidate has not worked as an ML Engineer for four years, has no chat-assistant or RAG experience, has not personally deployed a model as an API, and has no stated experience with monitoring or data versioning. The MSc is in Statistics rather than machine learning, computer science, or an engineering discipline. The candidate does show GCP experience, strong practical Python usage, orchestration through scheduled notebook jobs, and feature engineering, but not the full production-platform scope requested.
critique.improvement_instructions:
CRITICAL: In the second paragraph, make the workflow architecture and ownership boundary even more explicit by changing the final sentence to: "These projects have given me practical experience in Python and SQL, feature engineering, model evaluation, batch scoring, and orchestration through scheduled ML workflows on GCP." This uses the job's terminology without implying API serving or broader infrastructure ownership.

CRITICAL: In the third paragraph, clarify the nature of the engineering experience by changing "I have also added pytest unit tests for forecasting feature code, reaching approximately 60% coverage, and built and containerised a Python Streamlit application, writing its Dockerfile; the data platform team handled deployment to Cloud Run" to: "I have also added pytest unit tests for forecasting feature code, reaching approximately 60% coverage, and built and containerised a Python Streamlit application, writing its Dockerfile; the data platform team handled its deployment to Cloud Run." This preserves the truthful distinction between building the application/container and deploying it.

MINOR: In the opening paragraph, replace "AI systems that help merchants get support quickly and without friction" with "machine-learning systems that help merchants get support quickly and without friction." This avoids sounding as though the candidate has already built customer-support AI products while maintaining a direct connection to Quillstone's mission.

MINOR: In the closing paragraph, replace "my experience with forecasting, churn modelling and data workflows" with "my experience with forecasting, churn modelling, feature engineering, batch-scoring workflows and automated testing." This gives ATS and recruiters a more precise summary of the transferable experience already evidenced in the letter.

At Thistlebox, I developed a six-week-ahead recipe-demand forecasting workflow using LightGBM, orchestrated as scheduled notebook jobs in Vertex AI Workbench, with outputs written to BigQuery for operational reporting. The workflow improved WAPE from 23% to 14%, with an estimated 9% reduction in food waste. I also built a weekly XGBoost churn-scoring workflow in BigQuery and validated retention targeting with a holdout, where churn decreased by 2.1 percentage points in the treated group. These projects have given me practical experience in Python and SQL, feature engineering, model evaluation, batch scoring, and orchestration through scheduled ML workflows on GCP.

I have also added pytest unit tests for forecasting feature code, reaching approximately 60% coverage, and built and containerised a Python Streamlit application, writing its Dockerfile; the data platform team handled its deployment to Cloud Run. My MSc in Statistics, including a dissertation on Bayesian hierarchical models, supports my modelling and experimental-design work. I am now looking to develop further as an ML engineer, contributing careful testing, ownership and practical problem-solving as I deepen my production engineering experience.

Quillstone’s focus on support automation and its emphasis on team ownership, open sharing and learning from feedback make this role especially appealing to me. I would welcome the opportunity to discuss how my experience with forecasting, churn modelling, feature engineering, batch-scoring workflows and automated testing could contribute to the AI team.

Kind regards,
Tobias Mwangi-Hartley

critique.content_quality_feedback: The cover letter is clear, professional, well structured, and appropriately concise. It uses concrete evidence rather than generic claims, including the WAPE improvement from 23% to 14%, the estimated 9% food-waste reduction, the 2.1-percentage-point churn reduction, approximately 60% test coverage, and Cloud Run deployment ownership boundaries. The explanation of the transition from Data Scientist to Machine Learning Engineer is credible and appropriately candid. The main limitation is not writing quality but the substantial gap between the candidate’s current scheduled batch-ML experience and the role’s emphasis on customer-support AI, language models, production serving, monitoring, and data versioning.
critique.ats_compatibility_feedback: The letter is ATS-friendly: it uses conventional paragraphs, standard punctuation, readable terminology, and relevant keywords such as Python, SQL, GCP, BigQuery, Vertex AI Workbench, feature engineering, batch scoring, orchestration, pytest, Docker, Cloud Run, and automated testing. It should parse reliably. However, AI-screening probability for this particular vacancy is moderate to low because several high-priority terms from the advertisement are absent or cannot be truthfully added: chat assistants, RAG, language models, model serving, monitoring, data versioning, and the named MLOps tools MLflow, Kubeflow, and Airflow. The absence reflects genuine experience gaps rather than a formatting defect. The letter could also use the exact supported orchestration term “dbt Cloud Scheduler,” which appears in the candidate’s material but not in the letter.
critique.job_alignment_feedback: The strongest alignment is with Python, GCP, feature engineering, model evaluation, batch-scoring workflows, scheduled orchestration, automated testing, and practical ownership of ML-related projects. The culture paragraph also aligns well with Quillstone’s emphasis on ownership, open sharing, learning from feedback, and practical problem-solving. The candidate’s material shows a genuine transition toward ML engineering, but the role’s core must-haves create significant gaps: the candidate has an MSc in Statistics rather than a degree explicitly in machine learning, computer science, or engineering; has worked as a Data Scientist rather than an ML Engineer for four years; has not built chat assistants or RAG systems; has not independently deployed a model as an API; and has no stated experience with monitoring or data versioning. The candidate does have operational scheduled and batch workflows, but these should not be presented as equivalent to full production model serving or MLOps ownership.
critique.improvement_instructions:
MINOR, HIGH-VALUE IMPROVEMENT: In the third paragraph, make the supported orchestration experience more ATS-visible by changing “orchestration through scheduled ML workflows on GCP” to “orchestration through scheduled notebook jobs and dbt Cloud Scheduler on GCP.” This uses an exact tool name from the candidate’s material without implying experience with Airflow, MLflow, or Kubeflow.

MINOR, HIGH-VALUE IMPROVEMENT: In the second paragraph, make the operational nature of the work more precise by changing “I developed a six-week-ahead recipe-demand forecasting workflow using LightGBM, orchestrated as scheduled notebook jobs in Vertex AI Workbench” to “I developed and operated a six-week-ahead recipe-demand forecasting workflow using LightGBM, running it through scheduled notebook jobs in Vertex AI Workbench.” This better supports the advertisement’s language about building and operating ML systems while remaining truthful.

MINOR, HIGH-VALUE IMPROVEMENT: In the final paragraph, connect the candidate’s experience more directly to the role’s support-operations context without claiming customer-support AI experience. Change “could contribute to the AI team” to “could contribute to an AI team building reliable, measurable workflows for customer operations.”
